subject: Microbiology
vignette: A 58-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and a history of splenectomy after trauma presents with a 2-day history of fever, rigors, productive cough, and pleuritic chest pain. He is tachypneic and hypoxic. Chest radiograph shows lobar consolidation of the right lower lobe, and his sputum is described as rusty. Blood culture grows α-hemolytic lancet-shaped diplococci that are optochin sensitive and bile soluble.
question: Which of the following organisms is most likely responsible?

options.text: Enterococcus faecium
Streptococcus pyogenes
Streptococcus pneumoniae
Viridans group streptococci
Staphylococcus aureus

explanation_correct: Streptococcus pneumoniae is an α-hemolytic, lancet-shaped diplococcus that is optochin sensitive and bile soluble, and it produces rusty sputum with lobar pneumonia. Patients with functional or anatomic hyposplenia or asplenia are predisposed to overwhelming pneumococcal infection, and pneumococcal pneumonia is frequently severe in patients with chronic lung disease.

explanation_incorrect.A: Enterococcus faecium is catalase negative and grows in 6.5% NaCl with bile; it causes UTI, biliary infection, and endocarditis, not community-acquired lobar pneumonia.
explanation_incorrect.B: Streptococcus pyogenes is β-hemolytic, bacitracin sensitive, and PYR positive; pneumonia is not its classic presentation, which is pharyngitis and skin infection.
explanation_incorrect.D: Viridans streptococci are also α-hemolytic but are optochin resistant and bile insoluble, and they cause endocarditis rather than acute lobar pneumonia.
explanation_incorrect.E: Staphylococcus aureus is a catalase-positive, coagulase-positive coccus in clusters, and it classically causes pneumonia after influenza infection rather than rusty-sputum lobar pneumonia.

educationalObjective: Streptococcus pneumoniae is the optochin-sensitive, bile-soluble, encapsulated lancet-shaped diplococcus that causes rusty-sputum lobar pneumonia, especially in asplenic patients.

subject: Microbiology
vignette: A 24-year-old man with sickle cell disease and functional asplenia presents with 8 hours of fever to 40°C, confusion, and neck stiffness. He is hemodynamically unstable and requires fluids. He has had no pneumococcal vaccination in the last decade. Cerebrospinal fluid shows neutrophilic pleocytosis, high protein, and low glucose, and Gram stain shows α-hemolytic lancet-shaped diplococci.
question: Which of the following best explains why this patient is so susceptible to invasive infection with this organism?

options.text: Loss of IgA protease production by respiratory mucosa
Impaired T-cell help due to low CD4 count
Deficiency of complement C5 to C9 membrane attack complex
Impaired neutrophil oxidative burst from NADPH oxidase deficiency
Absence of splenic macrophage clearance of encapsulated organisms

explanation_correct: Anatomic or functional hyposplenia or asplenia predisposes patients to pneumococcal infection because the spleen clears encapsulated organisms through opsonin-dependent macrophage phagocytosis. Pneumococcus is heavily encapsulated and invasive infection is prevented mainly by capsular antibody and splenic function, which is the rationale for pneumococcal vaccination in asplenic patients.

explanation_incorrect.A: Pneumococcus itself makes IgA protease, so loss of mucosal IgA protease is not the mechanism; it is a virulence factor rather than a host deficiency.
explanation_incorrect.B: Low CD4 counts predispose to pneumococcal disease in advanced HIV, but the mechanism in asplenia is splenic clearance of encapsulated organisms, not impaired T-cell help.
explanation_incorrect.C: Terminal complement deficiency predisposes to recurrent Neisseria bacteremia and meningococcemia, not specifically to encapsulated pneumococcal disease.
explanation_incorrect.D: Defective NADPH oxidase causes chronic granulomatous disease, with catalase-positive organism infections such as S aureus and Aspergillus, and it is not the defect produced by splenectomy.

educationalObjective: Asplenia predisposes to overwhelming infection with encapsulated organisms such as Streptococcus pneumoniae because splenic macrophage clearance is lost.

subject: Microbiology
vignette: A 3-year-old boy in daycare has had 4 episodes of acute otitis media in the past year, each with fever, ear pain, and a bulging erythematous tympanic membrane. He is otherwise healthy and has no immunodeficiency. The pediatrician discusses pneumococcal vaccination, noting the current regimens given in early childhood.
question: Which of the following statements best describes the forms of pneumococcal vaccine available?

options.text: No vaccine exists because of antigenic variation of pili
Only a live attenuated oral formulation is available
Only a polysaccharide vaccine is available, given after age 18
A toxoid vaccine against the pneumolysin exotoxin is used
Both conjugate formulations (PCV13, PCV15, PCV20) and a polysaccharide formulation (PPSV23) are available

explanation_correct: Pneumococcal vaccines are available in both conjugate (PCV13, PCV15, PCV20) and polysaccharide (PPSV23) formulations. The conjugate vaccines are used in young children and the polysaccharide vaccine in older or high-risk patients. Because pneumococcal disease is capsule dependent, all of these vaccines target capsular polysaccharide.

explanation_incorrect.A: Absence of a vaccine because of pilus antigenic variation is the situation with Neisseria gonorrhoeae, whereas pneumococcal vaccines exist and target the capsule.
explanation_incorrect.B: There is no live attenuated oral pneumococcal vaccine; the vaccine-preventable organism with oral and intramuscular vaccine formulations is Salmonella typhi.
explanation_incorrect.C: A polysaccharide vaccine exists, but conjugate formulations are equally available and are the ones used in infants and toddlers.
explanation_incorrect.D: There is no pneumolysin toxoid vaccine in use; toxoid vaccines are designed against the toxins of diphtheria, tetanus, and pertussis.

educationalObjective: Pneumococcal vaccines target the capsule and come in conjugate (PCV13, PCV15, PCV20) and polysaccharide (PPSV23) forms.

subject: Microbiology
vignette: A 34-year-old woman presents with 4 days of maxillary facial pain, purulent nasal discharge, and fever. She has a history of recurrent sinusitis and one prior episode of pneumococcal meningitis. The microbiology laboratory is working up a respiratory isolate that is α-hemolytic and grows as lancet-shaped diplococci on blood agar.
question: Which of the following laboratory characteristics is most consistent with this organism?

options.text: Optochin sensitive and bile soluble
Optochin resistant and bile insoluble
Bacitracin sensitive with positive PYR
Growth in 6.5% NaCl with esculin hydrolysis
Novobiocin resistance with urease positivity

explanation_correct: Streptococcus pneumoniae is optochin sensitive and bile soluble, which distinguishes it from viridans streptococci, the other α-hemolytic group. It is encapsulated and lacks virulence without its capsule. Its classic clinical profile is MOPS: meningitis, otitis media, pneumonia, and sinusitis.

explanation_incorrect.B: Optochin resistance with bile insolubility identifies viridans group streptococci, which live in the oropharynx and cause dental caries and endocarditis, and they would not be identified with these pneumococcal findings.
explanation_incorrect.C: Bacitracin sensitivity with PYR positivity identifies Streptococcus pyogenes, a β-hemolytic group A organism rather than an α-hemolytic diplococcus.
explanation_incorrect.D: Growth in 6.5% NaCl with esculin hydrolysis is characteristic of Enterococcus and group D organisms, which are typically nonhemolytic and catalase negative.
explanation_incorrect.E: Novobiocin resistance with urease positivity is the signature of Staphylococcus saprophyticus, a coagulase-negative coccus in clusters from the urinary tract.

educationalObjective: Optochin sensitivity and bile solubility separate Streptococcus pneumoniae from viridans streptococci, and the capsular polysaccharide is required for virulence.
